items.title: 21.13 Role of Salt and Density in Ocean Circulation

source_refs.note: Topic 21.13 with the Dead Sea Tidbit and the Brain Teaser, answered (PDF 182); no figure. Answer needs review.

blocks.text: Ocean water contains a variety of dissolved substances, with salt the most abundant. The amount of salt in ocean water is called its salinity. Water with more salt is heavier, or denser, because the dissolved salt increases the mass of the water without significantly increasing its volume. So higher salinity leads to higher density.

In the ocean, density differences between water masses are among the key forces driving circulation, especially in deep waters. They arise mainly from differences in temperature and salinity: cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than less salty water. When surface water becomes colder and saltier, often through evaporation or the formation of sea ice, it becomes denser and sinks to deeper layers. As denser water sinks it pushes other water out of the way, creating slow-moving but large-scale currents that circulate through the world's oceans. This deep circulation transports heat and gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide around the globe, connects surface and deep water, and plays a critical role in regulating the Earth's climate.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: The Dead Sea is so salty that people float effortlessly in it: the density of its water is extremely high because of its salt concentration.

blocks.prompt: In the polar regions, seawater becomes saltier as ice forms. How does this affect ocean circulation, and what process does it drive?
blocks.explanation: When sea ice forms it leaves most of its salt behind, so the remaining water is colder and saltier, hence denser; it sinks, driving the deep part of the thermohaline circulation (the global conveyor belt).

items: Salinity: amount of dissolved salt; more salt means denser water.
Cold, salty water sinks; density differences drive deep ocean circulation, moving heat and gases.
